claims.text: Heating FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles in an inert atmosphere causes Cu to segregate to their surfaces.
Cu surface enrichment lowers the local melting point of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Melting initiates at Cu-enriched surface regions and subsequently propagates inward.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid and compositionally homogeneous, with a uniform elemental distribution.
Preferential diffusion during heating produces Cu-enriched surface regions.
The relatively low melting point of Cu drives Cu diffusion toward the nanoparticle surface.
Cu-enriched surface patches act as nucleation sites for localized melting.
Nanoparticles with significant Cu surface segregation will begin localized melting at a lower temperature than nanoparticles in which segregation is minimized.
Cu-segregated nanoparticles will exhibit surface-initiated melting detectable by in situ microscopy and DSC.
Nanoparticles with minimized Cu segregation will melt more uniformly.
Nanoparticles with minimized Cu segregation will begin melting at a temperature closer to the bulk-alloy melting point.
Compositionally uniform nanoparticles with minimal segregation exhibit homogeneous melting at a higher onset temperature characteristic of the bulk alloy.
Oxidation can alter the proposed melting behavior.
Significant variation in nanoparticle size can alter the proposed melting behavior.
The magnitude of the Cu-segregation-induced temperature shift and melting acceleration depends on particle size and processing conditions.
Surface passivation or vacuum annealing can suppress Cu segregation in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
